610.title: Simhika, the shadow-catcher
610.hook: a shadow-catcher drags Hanuman down, and the reason families read this book when life gets hard
610.carry: in hard times, families read the sundara kanda
610.howItsDone: Many Hindu families read the Sundara Kanda aloud in hard times, a portion a day, in Valmiki's Sanskrit or Tulsidas's Hindi; Simhika is the third being Hanuman meets over the sea.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a Hanuman the size of a thumb, and Surasa's rule and his promise, both kept at once.

Hanuman is flying fast, Surasa's blessing behind him, the sea open ahead. He has met a mountain and a serpent mother out here, and both of them he could see. Then, all at once, his speed fails. He's being held back, Valmiki says, like a great ship against a contrary wind. No storm, no wall, no monster. Every stretch of air takes more effort than the last, and when he looks around, there's nothing there.
screen: `HIS SPEED FAILS.` → `LIKE A SHIP AGAINST THE WIND.` → `NOTHING THERE.`

segments.voice: Hanuman looks up, down, left, right. Then he looks below, at the water, and sees her. A huge creature has risen from the sea: Simhika, a rakshasi, a demoness who catches flying things by their shadows. She has seized Hanuman's shadow where it falls on the waves, and through it she is dragging him down. And Hanuman knows what she is. Valmiki says he remembers: this is the shadow-catching creature Sugriva, the monkey king, warned the searchers about before they set out. So the slowing wasn't weakness. It had a name, and now he can face it. Simhika is not like Surasa. Surasa was a test sent by the gods. Simhika simply wants to eat whatever flies over her water. She opens her mouth wide, and Hanuman gets ready. Here's why this part of the story lives in Hindu homes. This book of the Ramayana, the Sundara Kanda, is one obstacle after another: a mountain, a serpent mother, a shadow-catcher, each one met and passed by a messenger flying for Rama. So when life gets hard, a sickness, a lost job, a long wait, many Hindu families read the Sundara Kanda aloud, a portion each evening, in Valmiki's Sanskrit or in Tulsidas's Hindi retelling. It isn't read as a spell. They're walking beside Hanuman through his troubles while they walk through their own: looking down, naming what holds them, and flying on.
screen: `SHE HAS SEIZED HIS SHADOW.` · `SUGRIVA HAD WARNED THEM.` · `ONE OBSTACLE AFTER ANOTHER.` · then, large: `READ IN HARD TIMES.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one hard thing you, or someone at home, is carrying right now. If you pray, say Rama's name, or a line you know to Hanuman, slowly, a few times, the way families do on Sundara Kanda evenings. If you don't pray, simply name the hard thing quietly to yourself, as Hanuman named Simhika, and breathe with it. Once it has a name, it can be faced.
Simhika. The rakshasi in the southern sea who catches flying creatures by their shadows, and drags Hanuman down until he looks below and recognizes her.
Your line: in hard times, families read the Sundara Kanda. Tomorrow, Hanuman meets her open mouth. That's day six hundred ten.

611.title: Strength with wisdom
611.hook: Hanuman answers a gift, a test and a danger three different ways, and why Hindus pray to him for wisdom
611.carry: pray to hanuman for wisdom, not only strength
611.howItsDone: Many families recite the Hanuman Chalisa, whose opening asks Hanuman for strength, wisdom and knowledge; readers of the Sundara Kanda point to the verse praising his steadiness, insight, intelligence and skill.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Simhika seized his shadow and dragged him down, until he looked below and knew her.

Simhika's mouth is open wide beneath him, the same trap Surasa set yesterday, only this time there's no blessing waiting at the end. Hanuman has one trick that already worked. Strong as he is, the question for him isn't how hard to hit. It's what this moment really is, and what it needs. Watch how differently he answers her.
screen: `THE SAME OPEN MOUTH.` → `NO BLESSING THIS TIME.` → `WHAT DOES THIS MOMENT NEED?`

segments.voice: Simhika opens her mouth wide, and at first Hanuman does what worked with Surasa. He makes himself huge, and she opens wider. Then he makes himself small and drops straight into her mouth. But this time he doesn't dart back out with a bow. Inside her, Valmiki says, he tears at her vital organs, then shoots out again, quick as thought. Simhika falls dead into the sea. The beings watching from the sky cheer, and they give him a line worth keeping: whoever has, as you do, these four, steadiness, insight, intelligence and skill, does not fail at the work. Set the three meetings side by side. Mainaka offered rest, and Hanuman answered with courtesy. Surasa set the gods' test, and he answered with wit. Simhika was simply a danger, and he answered with force. Same Hanuman, three answers, each right because he saw clearly first. That's why Hindus pray to Hanuman for more than muscle. The Hanuman Chalisa, the hymn so many families know by heart, opens by asking him for strength, wisdom and knowledge: bal, buddhi, vidya. In this tradition strength alone is never the ideal; the ideal is strength guided by wisdom. Then Hanuman looks ahead and sees it at last: the far shore, a line of hills, and beyond them a city. He comes down on a mountain at the water's edge, and Valmiki notes that after a hundred yojanas he isn't even out of breath.
screen: `INTO THE MOUTH, AND OUT AGAIN.` · `STEADINESS, INSIGHT, MIND, SKILL.` · `BAL, BUDDHI, VIDYA.` · then, large: `THE FAR SHORE.`

segments.voice: If you know the Hanuman Chalisa, or only its opening, say it slowly now, and when you reach strength, wisdom and knowledge, mean the middle one. If you don't pray, think of one choice waiting for you this week and ask only: what is this, really, and what does it need? Then let the breath come and go, steady, as Hanuman lands without being out of breath.
Simhika. The shadow-catcher whom Hanuman defeats from the inside, the third of three meetings over the sea, each answered in a different way.
Your line: pray to Hanuman for wisdom, not only strength. Ahead, a city waits for nightfall. Day six hundred eleven, done.

612.title: Small enough to serve
612.hook: the bravest monkey in the army chooses to be the size of a cat, and why Hindus see him as the model servant
612.carry: dasya: serve without needing to be seen
612.howItsDone: Many family shrines hold a picture of Rama's court, the Ram Darbar, with Hanuman kneeling at Rama's feet; devotees see him as the great example of dasya, devotion as service.

segments.voice: Yesterday: three meetings, answered with courtesy, wit and force, and your line: pray to Hanuman for wisdom, not only strength.

Hanuman stands on a hilltop at the edge of the sea, and in front of him is Lanka. A city on a mountain, ringed with golden walls, moats full of water, guarded gates, towers that seem to touch the clouds. Banners. Gardens. It is breathtaking, and it is very obviously a fortress. The monkey who just crossed an ocean in one leap stands still and thinks.
screen: `A CITY ON A MOUNTAIN.` → `GOLDEN WALLS, GUARDED GATES.` → `HANUMAN STANDS STILL.`

segments.voice: What Hanuman thinks about isn't how strong he is. It's how easily he could ruin everything. Valmiki lets us hear him reason. Rakshasas guard this city everywhere. If I'm seen in my own form, there'll be a fight, Ravana will be warned, and Sita may be put in greater danger. A messenger who shows off can wreck the very thing he was sent to do. So his plan is the opposite of a hero's entrance. He'll wait for night, make himself as small as a cat, and slip in unseen. The sun goes down. He shrinks and makes for the city, and as he goes, the moon rises, Valmiki says, like a swan gliding on a lake. The greatest leaper in the story chooses to be small, because the work is Rama's, not his. Hindu tradition has a name for this. Among the ways of loving God, the Bhagavata Purana lists dasya, devotion as service, and Hanuman is its great example: the servant who wants Rama's work done, not his own name shouted. It's why, in the Ram Darbar, the picture of Rama's court found in so many family shrines, the mightiest figure is the one kneeling at Rama's feet, hands folded. The Hanuman Chalisa sings this side of him too: he took a tiny form to appear before Sita.
screen: `HOW EASILY HE COULD RUIN IT.` · `AS SMALL AS A CAT, BY NIGHT.` · `DASYA: LOVE AS SERVICE.` · then, large: `KNEELING AT RAMA'S FEET.`

segments.voice: Fold your hands the way Hanuman does in the Ram Darbar. If you pray, offer one ordinary piece of today's work, a chore, homework, a shift, to God, with Rama's name or the name you use. If you don't pray, choose one task you'll do today for someone else without mentioning it. Breathe, and let it be enough that it gets done.
Lanka, Ravana's golden island city, which Hanuman enters by night, as small as a cat, because the work matters more than being seen.
Your line: dasya, serve without needing to be seen. Someone at the gate is about to notice him anyway. Until tomorrow.

613.title: A city full of music
613.hook: the city itself stops Hanuman at the gate, and inside, the enemy's capital is full of music and the Vedas
613.howItsDone: At Dussehra, many communities burn effigies of Ravana, and storytellers remember him as both a learned devotee of Shiva and the king who would not give Sita back.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lanka. Hanuman waited for dark, made himself the size of a cat, and went in by moonlight.

Hanuman, as small as a cat, reaches the gate of Lanka by moonlight. Before he can slip through, a figure steps out of the dark. She is huge and fierce, and she wants to know what a monkey is doing at her gate at night. Of all the guards in Lanka, she is the one who matters most. She is the city itself.
screen: `A FIGURE AT THE GATE.` → `SHE IS THE CITY ITSELF.`

segments.voice: She is Lanka, the city's guardian spirit, called Lankini in many retellings. She blocks his way, mocks him, and strikes him. Hanuman hits back but holds himself in: Valmiki says he uses only his left fist, not his full force. Even so, she falls, and from the ground she remembers an old warning from Brahma, the creator: when a monkey overpowers you, the end of the rakshasas has come. Go in, she says. Do what you came to do. Inside, Valmiki opens the city to us, and it's no cartoon lair. Mansions bright with lamps. Singing and instruments. And from some houses, the Vedas being chanted. Ravana himself is remembered in the tradition as a great scholar and a devoted worshipper of Shiva. Lanka is wealthy, beautiful, learned and alive, and somewhere in it a stolen woman sits grieving. That is the hard teaching here. In Hindu thought, learning, wealth and even prayer don't make a life good. Dharma does: doing what is right toward others. Ravana had the Vedas and still took Sita. That's why, at Dussehra, crowds burn the effigy of a scholar-king, not a cartoon monster, and many teachers read his ten heads as the vices that cleverness doesn't cure. Knowing much and doing right are not the same thing.
screen: `LANKA HERSELF AT THE GATE.` · `A CITY FULL OF MUSIC AND VEDAS.` · `LEARNING IS NOT DHARMA.` · then, large: `HE KNEW, AND STILL TOOK SITA.`

614.title: The wrong queen
614.hook: Hanuman thinks he's found Sita in Ravana's palace, then knows by her character that he hasn't
614.carry: sita is known, and honored, by her faithfulness
614.howItsDone: Many devotees greet one another with Jai Siya Ram, Sita's name before Rama's, and readers of the Sundara Kanda smile at Hanuman's leap of joy over Mandodari before he reasons from Sita's character.

segments.voice: Yesterday: rakshasa. The city's guardian fell and let him in, and inside, a capital full of music and prayer.

All night Hanuman has searched Lanka house by house, and every house has been the wrong one. Now he reaches the heart of the city, Ravana's own palace, glittering and guarded, and slips inside. In the innermost room he sees a woman so beautiful and regal that his heart leaps. After a hundred yojanas of sea and a city full of strangers, he's sure he has found her. He's about to celebrate too soon.
screen: `HOUSE BY HOUSE, ALL NIGHT.` → `THE INNERMOST ROOM.` → `HE'S SURE.`

segments.voice: Valmiki takes his time getting there. First Hanuman sees the Pushpaka, the flying chariot Ravana took from his half-brother Kubera, covered in jewels and seeming to float. Then a vast hall where Ravana's many wives lie asleep after a night of music, like a lake of lotuses closed for the night. Then Ravana himself, asleep on a magnificent bed. And near him, on a separate couch, a woman lovelier than all the rest, adorned and serene. Hanuman's joy explodes. He slaps his arms, kisses his tail, runs about, sings, climbs the pillars and jumps down again. He's a monkey, and for one moment he acts like one. Then he stops, and thinks. Sita, separated from Rama, would not sleep peacefully. She wouldn't wear jewels, or eat and drink at a banquet. She would never lie content in another man's palace. This is not Sita. It's Mandodari, Ravana's chief queen. He had only glimpsed Sita once, far off in the sky, as Ravana carried her past. So he corrects his mistake not by looking harder at a face, but by thinking about who Sita is: her grief, her faithfulness, her love for Rama. He knew her character before he knew her face. And that character is why Sita is honored in Hindu homes, not only as Rama's wife but as a goddess, whom many see as Lakshmi come to earth. Many devotees greet one another with Jai Siya Ram, victory to Sita and Rama, her name said first.
screen: `THE PUSHPAKA, THE FLYING CHARIOT.` · `HANUMAN'S WILD JOY.` · `SITA WOULD NOT SLEEP LIKE THIS.` · then, large: `JAI SIYA RAM: HER NAME FIRST.`

segments.voice: Think of Sita the way Hanuman did, by who she is: faithful, grieving, unbending. If you pray, say Siya Ram slowly with the breath, Siya on the way in, Ram on the way out. If you don't pray, think of someone you love and, instead of their face, call up how they are, one quality on each breath.

Your line: Sita is known, and honored, by her faithfulness. The search isn't over yet. See you tomorrow.

615.title: The root of good fortune
615.hook: having searched every room, Hanuman sits down in the dark and considers giving up, and then talks himself back up
615.carry: anirveda: don't let despair make the decision
615.howItsDone: Some who recite the Sundara Kanda in hard times dwell on Hanuman's despair and recovery here, and on the phrase anirvedaḥ śriyo mūlam, 'not despairing is the root of good fortune'.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ravana's palace, the flying chariot, the sleeping queens, and Mandodari, mistaken for Sita for one joyful moment.

Hanuman has searched Ravana's palace from end to end, room after room, and he hasn't found her. The night is wearing on. He has reached the end of the list, and he sits down. Sometimes the hardest moment isn't the danger; it's that. And Valmiki gives the hero of the Sundara Kanda something surprising here: a full, honest spell of despair.
screen: `THE END OF THE LIST.` → `HANUMAN SITS DOWN.`

segments.voice: First, a moment of conscience. Hanuman has walked among sleeping women, other men's wives, and looked at them. Has he done wrong? He thinks it through. His mind, he decides, was not disturbed: a woman must be searched for among women, and his intention was pure. Valmiki lets him weigh it rather than skip it. Then the despair. Maybe Sita is dead, he thinks. Maybe the rakshasas killed her. Early in it, Valmiki gives him a line in Sanskrit: anirvedaḥ śriyo mūlam. Not giving in to despair is the root of good fortune. He searches again, cellars, halls, corners. Still nothing. The despair comes back, deeper. If I go back without news, Rama will die of grief, then Lakshmana, then Bharata, then Rama's mothers, and on through Sugriva. He follows the chain of sorrow all the way down. For a while he even thinks of not going back at all, of staying by the sea as a hermit. Then, slowly, he turns. He bows in his heart to Rama and Lakshmana, to Sita, and to the gods, and begins again. The line didn't settle it once and for all. He said it, and still fell further. It's about what he did next, each time. Despair came and sat with him, and he didn't let it make the decision. This part ends with him looking out from the palace walls at a grove of trees he hasn't entered yet.
screen: `A MOMENT OF CONSCIENCE.` · `THE CHAIN OF SORROW.` · `ANIRVEDAH SHRIYO MULAM.` · then, large: `HE GETS UP AND SEARCHES AGAIN.`

segments.voice: If there's something you've been close to giving up on, let it come to mind gently, and don't argue with the discouragement; let it sit beside you, the way Hanuman's despair sat with him. Breathe with it. Then, on one breath, notice whether there's one place you haven't looked yet, one small next step, and just let it appear.
Ravana's palace. Where Hanuman searches every room and finds no Sita, sinks into despair, and rises again: not giving in to despair is the root of good fortune.
Your line: anirveda, don't let despair make the decision. Even heroes sit down sometimes. Day six hundred fifteen.

616.title: A flame veiled in smoke
616.hook: in a grove called without sorrow, Hanuman finds Sita, and Valmiki's picture of her: a flame veiled in smoke
616.carry: the light within is covered, never put out
616.howItsDone: Many Hindus light a diya for prayer at dawn or dusk, and Sita in the Ashoka grove is a familiar scene in Ramayana painting and performance; some devotees slow down at the moment Hanuman first sees her.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ravana's palace, every room searched, despair, and anirveda: don't let despair make the decision.

Hanuman leaps over a garden wall beside Ravana's palace, into birdsong, streams and shade. It's a whole grove of ashoka, a South Asian tree that flowers red and orange, planted for its beauty. In Sanskrit the name means without sorrow: a, not, and shoka, sorrow. It's Ravana's pleasure garden. And Hanuman is about to find a name that says the opposite of what it holds.
screen: `OVER THE GARDEN WALL.` → `ASHOKA: WITHOUT SORROW.` → `A NAME AND ITS OPPOSITE.`

segments.voice: Hanuman climbs a tall shimshapa tree, thick with leaves, near a clear pool. If Sita is here, he reasons, she'll come to this water for her prayers at dawn, the sandhya. So he hides in the branches and watches. And then he sees her. Valmiki describes her slowly, the way you'd describe someone you'd waited a long time to see. She is thin from fasting. She wears a single faded garment. She sits on the ground, sighing, surrounded by rakshasis with fierce faces. Valmiki gives two pictures: a flame veiled in smoke, and a thin crescent moon behind clouds. The light is still there; it's only covered. Hanuman knows her by her ornaments, which match those Rama described, and by her grief, exactly what he reasoned Sita's would be. Hidden in the tree, he weeps. That picture, fire under smoke, runs deep in Hindu teaching. The Bhagavad Gita uses it too: as fire is covered by smoke, so wisdom is covered by desire. Many teachers read it this way: the atman, the true self in every person, can be clouded by grief or wanting or fear, but it is never put out. So the week ends in the grove called without sorrow, with sorrow itself sitting on the ground, and the light inside her still burning.
screen: `UP THE SHIMSHAPA TREE.` · `A FLAME VEILED IN SMOKE.` · `KNOWN BY HER ORNAMENTS AND GRIEF.` · then, large: `COVERED, NEVER PUT OUT.`

segments.voice: Picture a small diya, the oil lamp lit at so many Hindu shrines, or light one if you have it. If you pray, bring to mind someone whose light seems covered right now, and offer them to God by name. If you don't pray, simply hold them in mind the way Hanuman watched Sita, steady and unhurried, trusting the light in them is still there.
Ashoka, the tree whose name means without sorrow, and Ravana's grove of them, where Hanuman, hidden in a shimshapa tree, finally sees Sita, and weeps.
Your line: the light within is covered, never put out. She doesn't know yet that help is in the tree. That's day six hundred sixteen.
